flashcards.q: Porter's Five Forces, and what they read?
flashcards.a: Supplier power, buyer power, threat of substitutes, threat of new entrants, rivalry. They read WHERE the profit pool sits and who holds power over your margins - e.g., a single model-API vendor = supplier power over your COGS and roadmap.

flashcards.q: Porter's sharpest one-liner about operational excellence vs strategy?
flashcards.a: 'Operational effectiveness is not strategy.' Teams on identical stacks (same models, same clouds, similar RAG) compete on efficiency; improvements diffuse and everyone converges to identical output at identical COGS - zero-margin rivalry. Strategy is a position others can't or won't occupy.

Network effects (user #4001 gets more value than #101), switching costs (data gravity, workflow embedment), economies of scale (chip design, $100M+ training runs), brand/trust, regulatory position, process/data flywheels (only if data is hard to replicate AND feeds real improvement loops).

flashcards.q: What is the moat attacker test?
flashcards.a: Name the well-funded attacker, their attack path, and the structural thing slowing them by YEARS not months. 'Better pedagogy' fails (they hire teachers); '3 years of per-student mastery traces that transfer across grades' might pass (replication needs time x students regardless of budget).

flashcards.q: State the working rules of build-vs-buy.
flashcards.a: (1) Buy everything that doesn't differentiate; (2) build only where ownership compounds a moat; (3) re-audit annually because utilities keep getting cheaper; (4) price exit BEFORE entry (abstraction layers, portable data). Fully-loaded eng cost ~$25-40K/month per engineer-month.

flashcards.q: Wardley map: axes, evolution stages, and what's reliable vs not.
flashcards.a: User needs on top, value-chain dependencies below; components placed genesis -> custom -> product -> commodity/utility. Evolution DIRECTION is reliable (things drift rightward as competition standardizes them); TIMING is not. Plays: commoditize a blocker, exploit competitor inertia.

flashcards.q: Platform vs product: the three tests before pivoting to platform.
flashcards.a: (1) Evidence of pull: unsolicited integration attempts/users scripting against endpoints; platforms are pulled rarely pushed; (2) toll enforceability: metering, billing, ToS teeth; (3) acceptance of the platform tax - backward compatibility forever, slow iteration. Most platform pivots from products die for lack of builders.

flashcards.q: Why are current LLM prices a fragile basis for any business case?
flashcards.a: Price per unit intelligence has fallen roughly 10x per 18-24 months across generations. Cases requiring prices to persist are fragile; drift favors strategies assuming cheap inference. Conversely self-hosting bets against the drift: serving engineering ~$1M+/yr vs API prices falling.

flashcards.q: When does vertical integration beat buying?
flashcards.a: When the component is critical AND markets can't supply required spec/scale at volume: Google TPUs ($100M+ design amortized fleet-wide), Apple silicon. Conditions: huge stable volume, differentiated requirements, tolerance for non-core expertise. Otherwise it's empire-building.

flashcards.q: Where do enterprise SaaS switching costs actually come from?
flashcards.a: Data gravity + integrations nobody rebuilds, workflow muscle memory across hundreds of users, config/permission archaeology, compliance audit history tied to incumbent, multi-year contracts with bundled discounts, migration-champion political risk. Jointly worth 20-40% price premiums.

flashcards.q: Should you open-source your core framework? The reasoning frame.
flashcards.a: Commoditizes YOUR component - rational when it blocks a competitor's complementary revenue, accelerates adoption toward monetized adjacencies (open-core hosting/enterprise tiers), or recruits talent; irrational when the component IS the differentiation. Post-2023 pick licenses deliberately (BSL shifts after cloud vendors absorbed OSS value); budget maintainership staffing.

flashcards.q: Feature vs product vs business - and why resourcing differs?
flashcards.a: Feature improves a host product (defended by host moats); product solves a need directly (needs acquisition+retention economics); business wraps products in durable economics (margins > COGS, retention > replacement, defensibility). Mislabeling features as businesses funds orphaned teams; promote AI-assistant feature to business investment only on independent retention + standalone unit economics.
